Show HN: Ekselio – Loveable for finance workflows (local first)
text:
Hi everyone, I am KD - Back in my college days, I dabbled with coding, learned the basics, HTML, CSS etc. but somehow I ended up in Finance which consumed the next 20 years. Then, during covid I picked up coding again, learned react, typescript, etc - even built a rudimentary site - and then came the chatgpt moment, followed by Claude etc.

So, as a side project, considering that I had spent 20 years in finance and M&A I started building Ekselio, loveable for finance workflows.

Differently from other vibe coding tools, this is local first - meaning the workflows are orchestrated by the LLM based on the file schema but then the execution happens in the browser - the cool thing is that you can see the canvas, the previews of each node, and the code base (SQl) - see the Canvas tab.

That said I did include a home tab, which is more of a visual, mainly because people think it's easier to relate to how folks operate, although I know finance and accounting folks usually like the workflow and full transparency - the other thing is that once you create a workflow you can save it and then next month,you can just click Run and it runs it again with no LLM tokes involved - so the infrastructure is minimal.

Everything can be exported in an excel data pack with M code in case someone would want to reproduce - think Audit ready. And, I also connected to quickbooks on line so someone can directly pull in and manipulate their financials live - I also connected to Fred which carries literally 800k series in terms of macro economic data - i.e. oil prices, inflation, CPI etc and finally to stocks.

I am hoping people find holes in the architecture or any ideas to make this flow a little bit better. It is in progress so if you run into bugs let me know. Considering that I am using my own API key, I have put a wall in case people overuse it but DM me if you would like to continue using, I can turn off the wall for you - hoping to keep that to a small number of users if I can and will do my best. Thank you again, appreciate you taking the time.

Show HN: RentBench – Levels.fyi for UK Rents
text:
My flatmate and I recently had our letting agent ask for a 30% rent increase on our London flat. Negotiating with them was hard given that there's a huge information gap: agents see rents across their whole portfolio and agreed deals, while tenants see a handful of listings whose asking prices may or may not reflect what people actually pay. This makes it easy for agents to justify big increases by saying "the market has moved", and really hard for tenants to prove that that's not the case. We even found that some neighbours in our own building are paying up to 30% more than others for similar flats.

This matters more now that England's Renters' Rights Act lets tenants challenge rent increases they believe are above market rate. The problem is there's no easy way for a tenant to find out what market rate is. Also, now that landlords can no longer accept offers above the asking price, they have an incentive to list higher than the rent they expect to get.

That's what inspired us to build RentBench, a platform where renters anonymously share what they currently pay and can see median rents for their area, so they can quickly check whether a price is in line with the market instead of spending hours going through listings. We also include official ONS rent inflation and median rent data for context.

It covers Great Britain for now, but we'd love to expand to other countries if people find it useful!

https://rentbench.fyi/

title: When oil prices spike, where does the money go?
text:
> a (large) price increase in one commodity would produce a general price increase.

Nope. Because if you spend more on one commodity, you necessarily spend less on other items. Spending less means less demand, and corresponding price reductions.

This is the Law of Supply and Demand at work.

Which also explains inflation - more money dumped into the economy, without a corresponding increase in the goods & services in the economy, devalues the money (see Law of Supply and Demand), which we call "inflation".

Money is not "special", and is subject to the LoSaD just like everything else.

Look what happened to Beanie Babies' prices when Tyco flooded the market with them. What do you think would happen to the price of Ferraris if Ferrari quadrupled production?

Why do you think Argentina's inflation is way down? It's the reduction in deficit spending. Do you think the Weimar Republic's trillion-to-one was caused by oil prices?

title: Japan moves to tighten rules for foreigners
text:
What a specious, fearmongering piece of tripe paraded as 'reporting'. One unnamed pseudonymous 'source' and another who is not in a position of risk due to her ability, albeit, reluctance to naturalize. All based on, we're worried because of political grandstanding by minority party members, and some second hand hearsay uptick in anti-immigrant sentiments around "Abdul".

Lets look at this for what it is; aljazeera making mud-pies and trying to sell them as cake.

None of the rules for work visas have changed; a proposal to reinforce financial readiness and social integration before permanent residency only leaves those working on a short term visa making regular renewals as they currently exist instead of transitioning to permanent resident visa.

Side-jobs and off-visa work continues to require formal approval for visa holders, "Designated Activities" is just some more paperwork, but in Japan the paperwork process is clearly defined and consistently followed. Foreign workers who find the system too complex or opaque need to hire a scrivener and be proactive about participating ahead of deadlines as there has never been a window for 'late' or 'overdue' paperwork.

The pay to cost-of-living margin is exceptionally good if you are not trying to outspend your neighbors; rent in most of the country equates to about 1/4 to 1/3 of a single MINIMUM WAGE full time job. And most employment for foreigners is better than minimum wage. The proposal to require above average income for permanent residency is simply to allow for more regular oversight of people working below the median in their industry, and makes sense as there have been cases of permanent resident visa holders falling below or behind on bills due to not being required to show that they have sufficient employment and not having the oversight that a visa renewal process would have provided.

Grandstanding aside, the only 'anti-foreign' sentiment statement i have encountered are in areas where foreigners have aggregated and behave outside of the safe and established norms; such as a taxi driver complaining that with the rise of outsiders he sees more jaywalking and he even stated it's not the ones who live here that make his day riskier, it's tourists. The overwhelming consensus here is that; qualified workers are scarce, the demand for help in agriculture, industry, hospitality, communications, and technology is real. The system can seem slow, but it is methodical not malicious, and the coworkers and employers are very happy to have willing help.

title: Intellectuals Are Fucking Idiots
text:
Central bank interest rates don't exist to 'control prices' per se. The state would like to create new money supply to make the economy move faster (e.g. maintain high employment in slow business periods). This would be to the disadvantage of the banks (their loans to debtors would be devalued). Hence a compromise was created to make the money supply more elastic without risking hyperinflation - banks may create new money supply for this purpose but must pay for it at the interest rate. Inflation is key a part of the feedback loop, to limit money creation to some supposedly optimal target range.

Surprisingly, this system was created by bankers and politicians, rather than economists /s

There are also many sources of 'cost of living' which are not related to money supply and therefore not directly related to monetary policy.

title: LinkedIn Larpmaxxing
text:
I got my current job (which I love and am being paid incredibly well for) by cold-firing a DM to someone at the company who I thought would be responsive who then put me down as a referral.

It's a whole song-and-dance, absolutely. The 'game' is to post enough (once/twice a week) with genuine, non-AI generated content to get your co-workers liking your posts and engaging. General, pro-social musings about layoffs, coworkers, job prospects, etc.

Recruiters started hitting me up fairly quickly after I started doing this even with my paltry engagement numbers (5k~ views per post) - half a dozen DMs a week for pretty decent roles in my city while I kept it up (and still a handful now after I stopped posting). And it also made my profile relatively 'attractive' for hiring managers, too, which is to say I didn't seem like a total sociopath with anger problems.

It helps that code-switching is pretty easy for me given my personal history so it doesn't feel like I'm somehow fundamentally betraying who I am by posting fluffy things on one social media platform. I imagine if you're more sensitive about your identity or how you engage socially, it can be very difficult to put any effort into your LI profile. If you've never had to put on a mask to fit in then the first wear can be very uncomfortable.

title: California farmers are struggling to sell grapes as demand for wine drops
text:
I think that trying to explain the reduced sales of California grape growers in terms of an international boycott of US products seems like highly motivated reasoning, not factual reasoning.

US exports have been growing every year since the pandemic low of 2020

US Exports (in billions of $)

   2025 $3,429.92
   2024 $3,232.52
   2023 $3,092.54
   2022 $3,058.45
   2021 $2,584.07
   2020 $2,172.85
   2019 $2,554.09
   2018 $2,544.58
We obviously do not have full data for 2026, but the first half is higher than the same time in 2025. But this is really driven by economic activity, so if there is a global recession, you can expect fewer people to buy US goods, just as you can expect Americans to buy fewer foreign goods. The 2020 low was not because of a boycott, but a general economic decline, and as far as I am aware, no boycott of US goods has ever been detected in the trade data, it's always been a media affair or hyperlocalized (e.g. some people boycotting Apple or Windows or Google seem to be the most common media stories).

And I think this is a pretty general situation, e.g. consumer boycotts rarely show up in trade data - to hit trade data you need government sanctions, nothing else moves the needle.

Car companies sell mostly the same car every year. They don’t have billions (or trillions) of dollars of debt riding on the next model they release being substantially better and cheaper (closer to profitability) than the previous one.

These AI companies have been selling AGI as coming any day for a while now. If it doesn’t arrive soon, the safety angle may be the only spin that keeps the massive (and required) investments pouring in.

If instead the narrative became that LLM progress was slowing, we’d almost certainly be looking at the next global recession.

At this point, there is too much money in AI for the truth to have much of a chance.

Why the Bronze Age Collapsed
text:
This is a thesis and it's not a new one.

It's true that when iron was first smelted and the first steel was made, it was structurally different to the Bronze economy. Iron is abundant and local. It doesn't require the same trade network (of copper and tin).

I'm surprised this article doesn't mention the Uluburun shipwreck [1]. It's archeologically important because it provides primary evidence of how extensive Bronze age trade networks were.

At best the author is theorizing not why the Bronze age collapse happened but why the empires and trade networks of that era didn't come back. But that's a different question.

We also have direct primary evidence from this time of the Sea Peoples [2]. To this day nobody really knows where they came from or why. Many modern scholars believe they may have been refugees themselves, possibly from natural disasters or droughts.

The most likely explanation for all this is that there was no single factor. All of these things likely contributed. It's still unclear why the collapse was so extensive and relatively sudden. That's not really satisfying but we've had fragile systems before that have collapsed suddenly and violently. Look at the outbreak of World War One as one major example.

One of my favorite phrases here is Outside Context Problem [3], which originates from the Iain M. Banks Culture novel Excession (love this book). It pretty accurately describes the collapses that happened in the Americas in the colonial era.

[1]: https://www.re-thinkingthefuture.com/case-studies/a9360-lost...

[2]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sea_Peoples

[3]: https://tvtropes.org/pmwiki/pmwiki.php/Main/OutsideContextPr...

title: Memory Companies Have Destroyed the Consumer Market
text:
Adam Smith was writing in the 1770s. At the time, only ~5% of the economy was capitalist. The rest was feudal, where lords owned the land and extracted rents.

Going from a feudal system to a capitalist system was great. All of a sudden people got payed wages, the creation of capital (productive goods) was incentivized. It created a much more dynamic economy.

What we are seeing now is a transition from capitalism to technofeudalism. You no longer buy things, you rent them from corporations that have much more power than you.

Additionally, the giant platforms (youtube, facebook, et al), are like a feudal lord's lands: people post / create content mostly for free, the lord extracts rents from the society (ads, etc). The many have no power, the lords get to organize their platforms however they want, prices rise because of the advertising spend, so even if you don't use facebook you bear the burden.

The entire point of anti-trust is to ensure a capitalist system doesn't transition back into a feudal one.

text:
Absolutely. Hence why manufacturing died long ago, and why the knowledge economy was already on the verge of death even before LLMs, and why we were already moving to the performance economy: because in the performance economy the consumer and the buyer are able to be disparate entities, where the buyers can have deep pockets even if the consumers don't.

In the performance economy it doesn't matter how rich the consumer is, but what the consumer wants to consume does matter. Because the buyer and consumer are disjointed in the performance economy, the consumer isn't swayed by cost. However, if the consumer prefers AI performances, which they quite easily could, then humans are in trouble. But so far it seems human performances remain what the consumer wants to consume.

(Technically manufacturing and knowledge work could have established the same separation, but since the bright minds went to performance nobody thought to before it was too late)

title: When oil prices spike, where does the money go?
text:
> a (large) price increase in one commodity would produce a general price increase.

Nope. Because if you spend more on one commodity, you necessarily spend less on other items. Spending less means less demand, and corresponding price reductions.

This is the Law of Supply and Demand at work.

Which also explains inflation - more money dumped into the economy, without a corresponding increase in the goods & services in the economy, devalues the money (see Law of Supply and Demand), which we call "inflation".

Money is not "special", and is subject to the LoSaD just like everything else.

Look what happened to Beanie Babies' prices when Tyco flooded the market with them. What do you think would happen to the price of Ferraris if Ferrari quadrupled production?

Why do you think Argentina's inflation is way down? It's the reduction in deficit spending. Do you think the Weimar Republic's trillion-to-one was caused by oil prices?
